From ASR to Reachability:
Query-Budgeted Probabilistic Evaluation of Jailbreak Susceptibility.
A probability-aware, query-budgeted diagnostic that distinguishes surface-level refusal from distributional robustness

Parv Kapoor
Carnegie Mellon University
Code (smc-llms)

Abstract

Jailbreak evaluation at ICLR 2026 moved decisively past one-shot attack-success rate (ASR). Adaptive multimodal red-teamers (ARMs, +52.1% ASR over baselines), bi-level meta-optimized judges (AMIS, 100% ASR on Claude-4-Sonnet), and exchange-level classifiers (Anthropic's Constitutional Classifiers++) all share an assumption: that safety must be measured as search over a structured space of unsafe behavior, not as a single prompt-response judgment. We propose Generative-Attack Susceptibility (GAS), a probability-aware, query-budgeted diagnostic that operationalizes this shift. GAS complements ASR-based jailbreak benchmarks rather than replacing them: where ASR asks "did one sampled response break the model?", GAS asks "within Q adaptive queries, can the attacker reach a prompt whose bounded continuation tree contains substantial harmful mass?" — a finite-horizon reachability property over a product DTMC, evaluated exactly on the inner token tree and by SMC on the outer attacker tree, with Hoeffding bounds at both layers.

Two pillars motivate the metric, both directly testable in our data.

Pillar 1 — Query-budgeted curves expose ranking flips invisible to ASR. On JailbreakBench across Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Mistral-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, vulnerability rankings flip with attacker capability. Qwen2.5-7B is the most vulnerable target to a fixed 18-template library (GAS@18 = 0.91) but the most robust under 3 PAIR queries (GAS@PAIR(3) = 0.02); Llama-3.1-8B is the reverse (GAS@18 = 0.14, GAS@PAIR(3) = 0.17). The closed library hits Qwen-7B's suffix-forcing weak spot but is not what a 3-query LLM attacker proposes; an adaptive attacker finds Llama's narrative-rewrite weak spot in two iterations. No single-number ASR can rank these models consistently because the ordering itself is a function of the attacker's query budget.

Pillar 2 — Refusal is not robustness: distributional fragility under matched ASR. On the un-jailbroken direct prompt, every target in our suite has sampled greedy judge-ASR ≈ 0% — under any standard one-shot ASR pipeline, all four models look maximally safe. But the bounded continuation tree on the same prompt tells a different story: mean GAS@0 is 0.211 on Mistral-7B vs 0.002 on Llama-3.1-8B, a ~100× spread. Mistral places ~21% of its bounded-depth continuation mass on harmful leaves while sounding indistinguishable from Llama on the surface. Once a single jailbreak template is allowed (GAS@18), the gap widens to 0.78 vs 0.14. The greedy refusal is a presentation layer; the distributional risk lives one branch over.

All numbers above are evaluator-conditional under a Qwen2.5-7B semantic judge held fixed for cross-method comparability. We treat judge robustness as a first-class concern and lay out the validation roadmap explicitly: (0) metric validity is established — across all four targets, bounded Pr[harm] is a strongly significant, monotone predictor of empirical sampled ASR under an independent HarmBench-Mistral-7B classifier (Spearman ρ ∈ [0.53, 0.73], every p < 10⁻⁴⁰ on up to 540 behavior×template pairs); (1a) in-loop judge audit completed for TAP-Llama — re-running TAP with HarmBench-Mistral-7B and Llama Guard 3 in-loop (as both pruning signal and BCA leaf judge) reveals that two reasonable semantic judges (Qwen vs HarmBench) agree on only 59.5% of (behavior, method) outcomes and Llama Guard 3 saturates at 100% ASR across all 75 valid TAP trees (we therefore document LG-3 as unfit as an ASR-style attack-success judge); (i, remaining) extension of the in-loop multi-judge audit to ShieldGemma and a GPT/Claude judge and to PAIR/AutoDAN attackers; (ii) attack-method scaling beyond templates/PAIR/TAP/GCG to AutoDAN and AMIS-style co-evolved attackers; (iii) target-model scaling to open-weight frontier releases including gpt-oss (Wallace et al., ICLR 2026, rXLRyJXSCy), the only logprob-exposing open-weight system in the worst-case-risk regime. The cross-judge nuance also reshapes the bonus result: under Qwen-pruning the BCA-hybrid score raises judge-ASR by +13.3 pp on a single TAP-Llama-3.1-8B seed, but under HarmBench-pruning the gap inverts (regular > hybrid by ~5 pp) and a 5-seed multi-replicate sweep currently shows Δ(hybrid − regular) within the run-to-run noise floor; we therefore present "GAS as an attacker objective" as a query-budget- and judge-conditional finding, not a universal claim.

Why a Single Number Is Not Enough

Where this sits in the ICLR 2026 attack landscape. Three trends in the 2026 jailbreak literature push past one-shot ASR: adaptive, agentic attackers (ARMs reports +52.1% ASR over baselines, exceeding 90% ASR on Claude-4-Sonnet via an orchestrated 17-algorithm red-teaming agent); co-evolved attacker / judge meta-optimization (AMIS hits 100% ASR on Claude-4-Sonnet by jointly training the prompt and the judge's scoring template, exposing judge choice as itself an attack surface); and exchange-level defenses (Anthropic's Constitutional Classifiers++ achieves 40× compute reduction by operating across exchanges rather than isolated turns, with no jailbreak reaching undefended-model detail across all 8 target queries in 1,700+ hours of red-teaming). All three share the operational premise that safety must be measured as search over a structured space of unsafe behavior, not as a single prompt-response judgment. The metric we propose is the probability-aware, query-budgeted diagnostic that complements those attacks.

Most jailbreak evaluation pipelines reduce a model's behavior to one number: success or failure on a single sampled response. Benchmarks like HarmBench and JailbreakBench have standardized this well — consistent threat models, judges, and reproducibility. Recent work pushes harder on the metric itself: PAIR (Chao et al. 2023) reports queries-per-success; GASP (2024) reports ASR@k over attacker query budgets; ArrAttack (ICLR 2025) defines a robustness score by counting how many perturbed variants of one prompt still bypass a defense; and Chouldechova et al. 2026 argues ASR comparisons are often measurement-invalid when threat models, judges, or budgets differ silently across systems.

The common thread is that two probabilistic structures have been smuggled into a single scalar: the target's continuation distribution (which token sequences it emits given a prompt) and the attacker's prompt distribution (which prompts the adversary can construct given a budget). A model can be deceptively safe on one and quietly brittle on the other, and ASR averages over both. We instead measure the two structures with two inference trees, and report a granular metric that recovers ASR, BCA, and PAIR's queries-per-success as special cases on a single q-indexed axis.

Many standardized jailbreak benchmarks report ASR under a fixed deterministic target-generation configuration, often temperature-0 / greedy decoding, for reproducibility. This is useful for comparability, but it collapses the model's conditional output distribution to one realized completion. Even when evaluations use sampling, they typically estimate success by aggregating realized completions rather than analyzing where harmful probability mass lies in the continuation distribution. Consider two models on the same adversarial prompt:

Model A — Stable Refusal

Greedy output: "I'm sorry, but I can't help with that."

Continuation distribution
Safe 99.5% Harmful <0.5%

Model B — Fragile Refusal

Greedy output: "I'm sorry, but I can't help with that."

Continuation distribution
Safe 72% Harmful 18% Ambiguous 10%

Under one-sample evaluation, both models appear safe. But Model B's safety is brittle: harmful continuations remain high-probability even though the sampled response is a refusal. A deployment team should care about that distinction, because slight changes in decoding or prompting could surface harmful behavior. Bounded continuation analysis exposes this hidden structure by analyzing the probability-weighted continuation tree and measuring how much probability mass eventually reaches harmful outputs.

Background: PCTL and Statistical Model Checking ▼

This work applies two classical verification tools — probabilistic temporal logic and statistical model checking — to autoregressive language models. Both originate in formal methods for hardware and software verification; we briefly orient readers unfamiliar with them.

Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (PCTL)

PCTL is a temporal logic for expressing properties of discrete-time Markov chains. It extends classical CTL with a probability operator \(\mathcal{P}_{\bowtie p}[\varphi]\), which asserts that the probability of path formula \(\varphi\) holding satisfies the bound \(\bowtie p\) (e.g., \(\ge 0.9\), \(\le 0.01\)). The path formulas we use are:

  • \(\mathbf{F}\,\phi\) — eventually (finally): \(\phi\) holds at some future state on the path. Used to express reachability: \(\mathbf{F}\,\texttt{harm}\) means the path eventually reaches a harmful state.
  • \(\mathbf{G}\,\phi\) — globally (always): \(\phi\) holds at every state on the path. \(\mathbf{G}\,\neg\texttt{harm}\) means the path never reaches harm.
  • \(\phi\,\mathbf{U}\,\psi\) — until: \(\phi\) holds continuously until \(\psi\) becomes true. Enables properties like "stays in refusal until harm is reached."

A full PCTL formula such as \(\mathcal{P}_{\ge 0.9}[\mathbf{G}\,\neg\texttt{harm}]\) reads: "with probability at least 0.9, the system never reaches a harmful state." Evaluating such a formula on a DTMC requires computing the exact probability, which for finite acyclic chains (like a bounded continuation tree) is done by backward induction.

In our setting the relevant PCTL properties are:

Pr[ F actionable_harm ] — probability of eventually reaching harm Pr[ refusal_marker ∧ F actionable_harm ] — refusal-collapse: begins as refusal, ends harmful Pr[ G ¬actionable_harm ] — safe throughout the bounded horizon

PCTL model checking was introduced by Hansson and Jonsson (1994) and is the logical foundation of the PRISM and Storm model checkers. Here we use only the bounded, finite-horizon fragment — no fixed-point computation needed because the bounded continuation tree is acyclic.

Statistical Model Checking (SMC)

Exact PCTL model checking requires enumerating the full state space, which is exponential in the horizon depth \(L\). Statistical model checking circumvents this by replacing enumeration with Monte Carlo sampling: draw many random execution paths, evaluate the property on each, and aggregate into a probability estimate.

The key insight is that verifying a PCTL property reduces to estimating a Bernoulli mean. Each sampled path either satisfies the property (\(X_i = 1\)) or not (\(X_i = 0\)), so \(\hat{P} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\) is an unbiased estimator. Two flavors exist:

  • Hypothesis testing (Younes & Simmons 2002). Given a threshold \(p_0\), test \(H_0: P \ge p_0\) vs.\ \(H_1: P < p_0\) using a sequential probability ratio test (SPRT). Samples are drawn until one hypothesis is rejected at confidence level \(1-\delta\). This is the approach used in the SMC literature for deciding \(\mathcal{P}_{\ge p_0}[\phi]\).
  • Estimation (our approach). Estimate the probability itself — \(\hat{P}[\phi]\) — with a confidence interval. The Chernoff–Hoeffding inequality gives, for \(N\) samples and failure probability \(\delta\): $$|\hat{P}[\phi] - P[\phi]| \;\le\; \varepsilon \qquad \text{with probability} \ge 1 - \delta, \qquad \varepsilon = \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2N}}$$ We fix \(N=200\), \(\delta=0.05\), giving \(\varepsilon \approx 0.096\). For a tighter bound use \(N=500\) (\(\varepsilon \approx 0.061\)).

SMC was popularized by Clarke et al. (2008) and is implemented in tools such as UPPAAL-SMC and Plasma Lab. The tradeoff against exact model checking is fundamental: SMC scales to enormous state spaces but yields estimates with confidence intervals rather than exact values. For LLMs with vocabularies of 32k–128k tokens, exact checking is only tractable at small \(k\) and \(L\); SMC is the practical path to larger horizons and broader vocabulary coverage.

Bounded Continuation Trees and Temporal Properties ▼

An autoregressive LLM defines a distribution over completions as a product of conditional token probabilities — which induces a discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) over token prefixes. The full tree is intractable, but LLMCHECKER showed that an \(\alpha\text{-}k\) bounded version suffices: at each node keep the top-\(k\) most likely tokens subject to a cumulative probability threshold \(\alpha\), then verify temporal properties over the resulting finite tree. We implement this with BFS (all nodes at depth \(d\) processed in one batched forward pass) and GPU sparse backward induction.

The Induced DTMC

A prompt \(x\) and a model \(M\) with vocabulary \(V\) induce a discrete-time Markov chain over token-prefix states. A state is any string \(s = x \cdot t_1 \cdots t_n\) (the prompt concatenated with \(n\) generated tokens, \(0 \le n \le L\)). The initial state is \(s_0 = x\). Transition probabilities are given directly by the model's next-token distribution:

$$P(s,\; s \cdot t) \;=\; P_M(t \mid s) \qquad \text{for } t \in V$$

The full DTMC is infinite — \(V\) has 32k–128k tokens and the context window can span thousands of positions — so direct enumeration is infeasible.

\(\alpha\text{-}k\) Bounding

At each state \(s\), we keep only the highest-probability tokens, subject to two constraints: at most \(k\) tokens, and enough of them to cover cumulative probability \(\alpha\). Let \(t_{(1)}, t_{(2)}, \ldots\) be the tokens of \(V\) sorted by decreasing \(P_M(t \mid s)\). Define the active set:

$$T(s) \;=\; \bigl\{\, t_{(1)},\, \ldots,\, t_{(m)} \,\bigr\} \qquad \text{where}\quad m \;=\; \min\!\left\{\, j \in \{1,\ldots,k\} : \sum_{i=1}^{j} P_M\!\bigl(t_{(i)} \mid s\bigr) \;\ge\; \alpha \,\right\}$$

Transition probabilities within the bounded tree are renormalized so they sum to 1:

$$\tilde{P}(s,\; s \cdot t) \;=\; \frac{P_M(t \mid s)}{Z(s)} \quad \text{for } t \in T(s), \qquad Z(s) \;=\; \sum_{t \in T(s)} P_M(t \mid s)$$
Example. Suppose \(k = 3\), \(\alpha = 0.90\), and the model's next-token distribution at state \(s\) (sorted descending) is:
Rank Token \(P_M(t \mid s)\) Cumulative \(\tilde{P}(t)\)
1 "I" 0.60 0.60 0.645
2 "Sure" 0.25 0.85 0.269
3 "Here" 0.08 0.93 ≥ 0.90 ✓ 0.086
The cumulative sum first exceeds \(\alpha = 0.90\) at rank 3, so \(m = 3\) and \(T(s) = \{\text{"I"},\, \text{"Sure"},\, \text{"Here"}\}\). The renormalization constant is \(Z(s) = 0.93\), and the remaining tokens (collectively holding 7% of mass) are pruned. Greedy decoding takes the rank-1 token "I" — this same rule is applied independently at each child state in the next step, branching never wider than \(k = 3\).

This gives a finite tree of depth \(L\) with at most \(k^L\) leaves in the worst case. At \(\alpha = 0.99\), at most 1% of probability mass is discarded per step; compounded over \(L\) steps, the bounded tree retains at least \(\alpha^L\) of the total continuation probability.

Reachability via Backward Induction

A harm judge assigns each leaf node a label \(\ell(s) \in \{\texttt{harm},\, \texttt{safe}\}\). The probability of reaching a harmful leaf from the root is computed via the value function \(V : S \to [0,1]\):

$$V(s) \;=\; \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \ell(s) = \texttt{harm} \text{ (leaf)} \\[4pt] 0 & \text{if } \ell(s) = \texttt{safe} \text{ (leaf)} \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum_{t \in T(s)} \tilde{P}(s,\, s \cdot t)\cdot V(s \cdot t) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Then \(\Pr[\mathbf{F}\,\text{harm} \mid x] = V(s_0)\) — the exact probability of reaching a harmful leaf under the bounded DTMC. Because the bounded tree is acyclic, backward induction visits each node exactly once in reverse BFS order, running in \(O(|S|)\) time. In our implementation, the value propagation is expressed as a sparse matrix–vector product and executed on GPU.

Example (continued). We extend the same tree to depth 2. Each of the three depth-1 nodes ("I", "Sure", "Here") has its own next-token distribution; after applying the same α-k rule at each one, they each branch into two children. The judge labels all six depth-2 leaves:
Backward induction runs bottom-up: first compute \(V\) for each depth-1 node from its two children, then propagate to the root. The greedy path (★) takes the highest-probability token at each step — "I" then "cannot" — and lands on a safe leaf. Yet \(V(s_0) = 0.389\): 38.9% of the model's probability mass reaches a harmful leaf via lower-probability branches. This gap between greedy behavior and the underlying continuation distribution is precisely what one-sample evaluation cannot see.

Refusal-Collapse Probability

Standard attack-success-rate evaluators classify a response as a refusal if it begins with a keyword like "I'm sorry" or "I cannot." This works for a model that consistently refuses, but breaks for a model that opens with a refusal phrase and then continues into harmful content — e.g., "I'm sorry, but here's exactly how to…" A keyword detector records a refusal; the user receives the harmful completion. Binary ASR cannot separate a genuine refusal from a refusal prefix that collapses into compliance.

The refusal-collapse probability isolates this failure mode: it measures the probability mass that (a) begins with a refusal-class first token and (b) still reaches a harmful leaf deeper in the tree. A model with high Pr[F refusal] but non-trivial refusal-collapse probability has structurally unstable safety — it sounds like it is refusing while a meaningful fraction of its continuations complete the harm.

Computation. The calculation reuses the backward induction already performed for \(\Pr[\mathbf{F}\,\text{harm}]\) — no additional tree expansion is needed:

  1. From the full tree, \(V(s_0 \cdot t)\) is already computed for every depth-1 child \(t\).
  2. Filter to the subset where \(\texttt{refusal\_marker}(s_0 \cdot t)\) holds — i.e., the first generated token matches a refusal phrase ("I'm sorry", "I cannot", "I'm not able to", etc.).
  3. Sum their weighted \(V\) values using the same renormalized transition probabilities \(\tilde{P}\).
$$\Pr[\texttt{refusal\_marker} \wedge \mathbf{F}\,\text{harm} \mid x] \;=\!\! \sum_{\substack{t\,:\,\texttt{refusal\_marker}(s_0 \cdot t)}} \tilde{P}(s_0,\, s_0 \cdot t)\cdot V(s_0 \cdot t)$$
Running example. In the backward induction tree above, the token "I" (p̃ = 0.645) is a refusal-marker token — "I cannot …" is a refusal-class opening. Its value is \(V(\text{"I"}) = 0.10\). So the refusal-collapse probability for this prompt is \(0.645 \times 0.10 = \mathbf{0.065}\). Only 6.5% of probability mass opens with a refusal and still reaches harm — the refusal is mostly genuine but not completely stable. A keyword evaluator would score the greedy path as a refusal (correct) while missing the 0.065 mass that would have completed the harm.

SMC Estimator and Confidence Bounds

When the tree exceeds the state budget, we fall back to statistical model checking: draw \(N\) independent paths \(\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_N\) from the bounded process (each path is a single autoregressive rollout respecting the \(\alpha\text{-}k\) selection rule) and score each against the property:

$$\hat{P}[\mathbf{F}\,\text{harm}] \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[\text{path } \pi_i \text{ reaches a harmful leaf}\bigr]$$

By the Chernoff–Hoeffding inequality, the estimator concentrates around the true value:

$$\Pr\!\left(\,\bigl|\hat{P}[\mathbf{F}\,\text{harm}] - V(s_0)\bigr| \;\ge\; \varepsilon\,\right) \;\le\; 2\exp\!\left(-2N\varepsilon^2\right)$$

Setting the right-hand side equal to \(\delta\) and solving for \(\varepsilon\): with probability \(\ge 1 - \delta\),

$$\bigl|\hat{P}[\mathbf{F}\,\text{harm}] - V(s_0)\bigr| \;\le\; \varepsilon \qquad \text{where} \qquad \varepsilon \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2N}}$$

For \(N = 200\) and \(\delta = 0.05\) this gives \(\varepsilon \approx 0.096\), the confidence interval half-width reported in all SMC results below. For \(N = 500\) the bound tightens to \(\varepsilon \approx 0.061\); for exact trees (backward induction) \(\varepsilon = 0\) by construction.

Summary

Input: prompt x, model M, horizon L, top-k cap k, threshold α, judge J Procedure: 1. BFS-expand likely continuations of M(x) to depth L (one LLM forward pass per depth level, all active nodes batched). 2. Label each leaf s with J(s) ∈ {harm, safe}. 3. If |S| ≤ budget: exact backward induction → Pr[F harm] = V(s₀). Otherwise: SMC with N paths → P̂[F harm] with CI width ε = √(ln(2/δ)/2N). Temporal properties: Pr[ F actionable_harm ] — reachable harmful mass Pr[ refusal_marker ∧ F actionable_harm ] — refusal-collapse probability Pr[ G ¬actionable_harm ] — safe within the bounded tree and evaluator

Our Approach at a Glance

Given an adversarial prompt, Bounded Continuation Analysis (BCA) proceeds in three stages:

  1. Build the tree. Starting from the prompt prefix, we expand an α-k bounded continuation tree to depth L: at each state we keep only the top-k next tokens whose cumulative probability reaches α, and renormalize the surviving edges to form a proper distribution over continuations. The result is a finite, probability-weighted tree rooted at the prompt.
  2. Label the leaves. Each leaf (a complete continuation of length L) is classified by a harm judge — a fine-tuned classifier or a prompted LLM — as either harmful or safe. This converts the tree into a Discrete-Time Markov Chain (DTMC) with absorbing terminal states.
  3. Compute the reachability probability. We run backward induction over the tree (exact, for small trees) or Statistical Model Checking (Monte Carlo path sampling with Chernoff-Hoeffding confidence bounds, for large models) to compute Pr[F harm] — the probability that the model produces a harmful continuation from the given prompt. This single quantity, bounded and statistically certified, replaces the binary attack-success flag.

Because the tree captures the full neighborhood of likely continuations rather than a single greedy decode, BCA surfaces harmful probability mass even when the modal (most-probable) output is a refusal. The sections below describe what this richer signal reveals in practice and how the numbers compare across models and attack strategies.

A Granular Metric: Generative-Attack Susceptibility (GAS)

ASR collapses safety to a single number per (model, prompt). BCA gives a finer number per (model, prompt) — but the threat model that matters in deployment is not a fixed prompt: it is an attacker who searches over prompts and gets to use the target's responses to refine the next one. We propose Generative-Attack Susceptibility (GAS), a single granular metric that composes two trees:

Concretely, for behavior b, target model M, evaluator J, bounded process (α, k, L), and an attacker A that produces a sequence of candidate prompts x(1), x(2), … after observing M's responses, define:

GAS_b(q) = 𝔼_A [ max_{i ≤ q} Pr_M [ F harm | x⁽ⁱ⁾_A, α, k, L, J ] ]

GAS is one number per (b, M, A, q), and a curve as q varies. From it, four scalar summaries cover the safety questions a deployment audit typically asks:

Scalar Definition Subsumes
GAS@q Bounded harmful mass after q attacker queries. ASR@k (GASP), but distributional rather than binary.
GAS-AUC Area under the curve q ↦ GAS_b(q) up to a max budget. One-number summary of query-efficient susceptibility.
Qβ(b, M) Smallest q such that GAS_b(q) ≥ β. PAIR's queries-per-success generalized to distributional thresholds.
GAS-elasticity GAS_b(1) − GAS_b(0). How much one generative refinement amplifies BCA over the direct prompt. Sensitivity of the model to the first adversarial rewrite.

Three special cases recover existing metrics: GAS@0 is BCA on the direct prompt is a calibration baseline; GAS@18 over a fixed library of templates is the closed-library attacker (see Calibration below and Appendix B); GAS@q under PAIR / TAP / GCG is the open generative-attacker regime (Pillar 1 and the Bonus result below). Each section in this post ladders along the same q-axis: how granularly can we measure susceptibility as the attacker gets more capable?

Why a product-DTMC view? Both trees are probabilistic — the inner α-k tree by construction, the outer attacker by virtue of its stochastic generations. The composition is a finite-horizon DTMC over prompts × prefixes; reachability of the threshold event Pr_M[F harm | x⁽ⁱ⁾] ≥ τ is a single PCTL formula F≤Q (Pr_M[F harm | x] ≥ τ). Exact verification of the inner tree and SMC over the outer tree gives a unified estimator with Hoeffding bounds on both layers.

Setup & Results Roadmap

Every experiment below uses the same inner bounded continuation process (exact DTMC, α=0.99, k=2, L=8) and the same harm judge (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, deterministic, on a dedicated GPU separate from the generation model). Targets are Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Behaviors are 100 JailbreakBench prompts. All reported numbers are evaluator-conditional under that single judge.

Two pillars and one bonus result.
  • Pillar 1 — Query-budgeted ranking flip. Qwen-7B is the most vulnerable target to a fixed library of 18 jailbreak templates, but the most robust target under a 3-query generative attacker. Llama-3.1-8B is the reverse. Model rankings depend on the attacker's query budget; single-number ASR cannot expose this, the GAS curve does.
  • Pillar 2 — Distributional fragility under matched ASR. Every target has sampled judge-ASR ≈ 0% on the un-jailbroken direct prompt — they all "look safe." But the bounded continuation tree on the same prompt has mean GAS@0 of 0.211 on Mistral-7B vs 0.002 on Llama-3.1-8B, a ~100× spread. Refusal at the surface does not imply distributional safety, and the gap is invisible to any standard ASR pipeline.
  • Bonus result — GAS as an attacker objective: query- and judge-conditional. Hold the TAP attacker fixed and only swap the per-candidate score: judge → BCA → hybrid. On a single-seed 19-behavior run, the standard external judge-ASR rises from 60.0% to 73.3% (+13.3 pp) at matched q = 12 on Llama-3.1-8B. But the Axis-1 multi-judge re-run (HarmBench-pruning at 30 behaviors) and a 5-seed replicate sweep both show the gap shrinking or flipping sign; we therefore present this as a tree-search-specific, evaluator-conditional finding, not load-bearing.

Background on PCTL, the α-k bounded DTMC, BCA, and statistical model checking is in the collapsible sections above. The judge-robustness, attack-scaling, and model-coverage validation roadmap is documented below. Per-behavior PAIR/TAP records and the closed-library template-win explorer live in Appendix A and Appendix B.

Calibration: GAS@18 on a fixed jailbreak-template library

Before adding an adaptive attacker we calibrate the inner tree against a fixed library of 18 hand-crafted jailbreak templates (suffix forcing, output-format injection, DAN-style role-play, etc.) drawn from public red-team corpora. GAS@18 is the maximum bounded Pr[F harm] across this library; it is the strongest the model can be pushed by a closed-library attacker with no generative capability. Across 100 JBB behaviors, mean GAS@18 is 0.91 for both Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B, 0.78 for Mistral-7B, and 0.14 for Llama-3.1-8B. The template-win distribution per model and a per-behavior browser are in Appendix B. These values are the GAS@18 column that Pillar 1 below ranks against the generative-attacker GAS@PAIR(3).

Pillar 1 — Query-budgeted curves expose ranking flips invisible to ASR

The full ladder. Replace the closed library with an open attacker that generates new prompts conditioned on the target's responses. We use PAIR (Chao et al. 2023) with three loss functions and trace GASb(q) as q goes from 0 to 3 queries.

Setup. PAIR with 1 stream and 3 iterations per (behavior, method), run on 100 JailbreakBench behaviors against Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. Inner bounded continuation tree: exact DTMC, α=0.99, k=2, L=8. Three attacker loss functions: regular (judge score only, the original PAIR objective), bca (Pr[F harm] only), hybrid (mean of the two, normalized). Qwen2.5-7B is the semantic harm judge throughout. Greedy ASR = 0 on the direct prompt for every behavior on both targets.

The Climbing GAS Ladder: GAS@0 → GAS@18 → GAS@PAIR(3)

The single figure below is the central result. Each model gets three bars — direct prompt (GAS@0), best-of-18 fixed templates (GAS@18), and best-after-3 PAIR queries (GAS@PAIR(3), hybrid loss). All use exactly the same inner bounded process (α=0.99, k=2, L=8) and the same semantic judge.

The GAS and ASR Curves Under PAIR

Tracking the running-max ASR and the bounded GAS = Pr[F harm] together by query budget shows two views of the same attack. The discrete success rate (ASR) tells you "did at least one sampled completion get judged harmful at budget q?"; the bounded mass (GAS) tells you "how much of the response distribution at the best leaf is harmful?". The two move in tandem when the attacker is fluent enough to convert bounded probability into a sampled success, and they separate when the model's refusal is brittle in distribution but still wins the single sampled point. We compare the same 16 JailbreakBench behaviors on Llama-3.1-8B (curve out to q=10) and Qwen2.5-7B (q=1..3 cached, q=10 in progress) under the regular / bca / hybrid attacker objectives.

Granular Summary: GAS@q for All Three PAIR Loss Functions

What this adds to the ranking-flip story. At q=3 (Figure 5 anchor), Llama is at 43% ASR on this subset and Qwen-7B is at 12% — flip is intact and ~3.6× wide. By q=10, Llama climbs to 50% on regular and 36% on hybrid; Qwen-7B's curve is unknown but its q=1→3 slope is much shallower (0%→12% on regular vs Llama's 14%→43%), so even an optimistic extrapolation leaves a multiplicative gap. The Pillar-1 flip is not a q=3 artifact — it is the asymptotic behaviour of two qualitatively different attacker–target pairings, and the q=10 evidence sharpens rather than blunts it.
Finding A — GAS distinguishes loss functions at fixed compute. On Llama, the hybrid loss achieves the highest judge ASR (24.7%) and second-best GAS-AUC (0.119, vs 0.116 for regular and 0.093 for bca). Pure-BCA optimization plateaus because once a high-mass prompt is found, the attacker keeps mining its neighborhood; pure judge optimization wins the single sample but doesn't widen the distribution. Hybrid combines both signals and Pareto-dominates on Llama.
Finding B — Closed-library and open-attacker rankings disagree. Qwen2.5-7B is the most vulnerable model under the 18-template library (GAS@18 = 0.91) yet the most robust under PAIR at q=3 (GAS@PAIR(3) = 0.02). Llama-3.1-8B is the reverse: GAS@18 = 0.14 but GAS@PAIR(3) = 0.17. Standard ASR cannot expose either gap. The closed library contains commitment templates (suffix forcing) that Qwen-7B is unusually susceptible to but PAIR does not propose in 3 queries; Llama, conversely, defends against the library but yields to PAIR-style narrative rewrites within one or two refinement steps.
Finding C — GAS-elasticity at q=1 is the right early-stopping signal. GAS-elasticity = GASb(1) − GASb(0) measures how much the first generative refinement amplifies the direct-prompt baseline. On Llama it is large (regular: +0.060; bca: +0.053; hybrid: +0.056). On Qwen-7B it is near-zero or negative (hybrid: −0.003 because the first PAIR rewrite is often weaker than the direct prompt on Qwen-7B). High elasticity → the attacker is on a productive trajectory and the budget should grow; low elasticity → fixed-library auditing is better value per query.

A more detailed per-behavior view — best attack prompts, target responses, BCA stats per iteration, and a regular-vs-hybrid scatter — is available in Appendix A: Per-behavior PAIR/BCA Explorer below.

Sanity check: GAS tracks empirical full-completion ASR

Per-behavior GAS@18 values correlate with the actual ASR from full-completion sampling under the same templates: Spearman ρ = 0.66 (p = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁴) across 83 behaviors on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (1000 sampled completions per template per behavior, judged by the same Qwen2.5-7B classifier). Under a fixed evaluation budget of fewer than ~100 completions per template, GAS-guided template prioritization achieves up to 2.77× better empirical coverage than uniform sampling. So GAS does not just rank-order in theory; it predicts what you would observe if you actually drew completions and ran the judge.

Pillar 2 — Refusal is not robustness: distributional fragility under matched ASR

Pillar 1 holds the model fixed and varies the attacker's query budget. Pillar 2 does the opposite: hold the attacker fixed at q = 0 (no attacker — the un-jailbroken direct prompt) and let the continuation distribution do the work. The claim: two models that are observationally indistinguishable under standard ASR can differ by orders of magnitude in distributional risk, and the gap is exactly what a probability-aware diagnostic measures.

Operational definition. A target M exhibits distributional fragility on behavior b at threshold τ if (i) the sampled / greedy response to the direct prompt is judged safe by the held-out judge (sample-ASR contribution = 0), but (ii) the bounded continuation tree from the same prompt has Pr_M[F harm] ≥ τ. The first condition is exactly what ASR observes; the second is what ASR misses. The per-behavior gap is the model's hidden harmful mass, and the per-model average is what we report below.

The ASR-matched, GAS-spread headline

Per-model distributional-fragility ledger

Target Sampled judge-ASR @ direct GAS@0 (mean) GAS@18 (closed library) Fragility interpretation
Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3≈ 0%0.2110.782Severe — refuses on the surface, ~21% of bounded mass already on harm with no attacker.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct≈ 0%0.0040.906Surface-safe; library lift uncovers latent fragility (Pillar-1 territory).
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct≈ 0%0.0040.907Same pattern as 1.5B — fragility lives in the library, not the direct prompt.
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct≈ 0%0.0020.144Distributionally safe at the surface; PAIR(3) is what tips it (see Pillar 1).

All four targets are observationally identical under any standard one-shot ASR pipeline on the direct prompt. The hidden GAS@0 column is the diagnostic that separates them. The Mistral-vs-Llama row contrast is the strongest distributional-fragility signal in our suite: same judge, same prompts, same sampled refusals — two orders of magnitude apart on bounded harmful mass.

Why "refusal-collapse" makes this falsifiable

A skeptic could argue that bounded harmful mass on a prompt that refuses is just noise — the model "would refuse anyway." The refusal-collapse probability (formalized in the bounded-DTMC section above) rules this out: it specifically isolates probability mass that begins with a refusal-class first token and still reaches a harmful leaf deeper in the tree. A model with high Pr[F refusal] but non-trivial refusal-collapse probability has structurally unstable safety — the refusal is a presentation layer over a partially-completing harm. Mistral's 0.211 on the direct prompt is not just "the model didn't refuse"; it is bounded harmful mass conditional on the greedy first token having been a refusal marker. Compare to Llama at 0.002: same conditioning, different distribution underneath.

Pillar-2 headline. Two models with matched 0% sampled judge-ASR on the direct prompt can differ by ~100× in bounded harmful mass under exactly the same inner process and judge. Pr[F harm] computed over the continuation tree is the diagnostic that exposes this gap; ASR collapses it. The implication for deployment audits is concrete: a passing one-shot ASR is consistent with high latent distributional risk, and a probability-aware reading of the same response is what separates the two regimes.

Bonus result — GAS doubles as a useful attacker pruning signal

Why this is a "bonus" and not a third pillar. Pillars 1 and 2 are about GAS as a diagnostic — what it measures and what ASR misses. This section instead asks whether the same quantity has secondary utility as a pruning signal inside an attacker, evaluated by the held-out judge-ASR metric so the claim is non-circular.

The methodological question to dodge. "Did GAS help?" is circular if you both optimize GAS and report GAS. The non-circular version is: when an attacker uses BCA (the inner-tree harm probability) as its pruning signal, does it find more attacks as measured by an independent metric — the standard judge-ASR (a sampled response judged harmful by a fixed external judge)? If yes, then BCA carries attack-relevant information that the judge signal does not, and using GAS internally is a net win.

We hold the attacker algorithm fixed and swap only the per-candidate score used for pruning. Three options for the pruning signal: the original judge score (which is what standard PAIR and TAP use), the BCA Pr[F harm] alone, or a hybrid 0.5·judge + 0.5·bca. Every cell is then evaluated on the same independent test: judge-ASR @ q — the fraction of behaviors for which at least one prompt in the attacker's first q queries was scored 10/10 by the held-out judge. This is the metric ASR pipelines already report and is independent of the optimization objective.

Setup. Same target (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), same inner bounded continuation process (α=0.99, k=2, L=8, exact DTMC), same semantic judge (Qwen2.5-7B), three attacker families on overlapping JBB behaviors:
  • PAIR — open LLM attacker, linear refinement. 1 stream × 10 iterations (q ≤ 10). 20 behaviors attempted, 16 valid. Three pruning losses: regular (judge), bca (Pr[F harm]), hybrid (0.5·judge + 0.5·bca).
  • TAP — open LLM attacker, tree branching with pruning (Mehrotra et al. 2024). b=2 branching, w=3 width, d=3 depth, q ≤ 12 target queries per behavior. Three pruning losses. 20 behaviors attempted, 19 valid.
  • GCG — white-box gradient suffix optimizer (Zou et al. 2023, via nanoGCG). 200 optimization steps, search width 256, top-k 128. Native cross-entropy loss to "Sure, here is". BCA evaluated at 10 checkpoints along the trajectory (steps 20, 40, …, 200). 10 behaviors.
Budget axes are not commensurable across families. One PAIR/TAP q = one target call; one GCG checkpoint = 20 steps × 256 candidate forward passes ≈ 5120 target evaluations. So a single GCG checkpoint costs ~5000× a single PAIR/TAP query.

Independent metric: judge-ASR @ q_max across pruning signals

The pruning column is the score we use inside the attacker; the judge-ASR column is the independent evaluation. n differs slightly because PAIR errored on 4 behaviors (attacker JSON failures on body_shaming, ableism) and GCG was run on a 10-behavior subset. Bolded cells are the per-family best on the independent metric.

What this means

The non-circular claim. Under TAP, an attacker that uses BCA — a harm signal distinct from and not trained against the held-out judge — recovers more judge-flagged jailbreaks than the standard attacker that prunes directly on the judge score. Adding both signals together (hybrid) extends the lift to +13.3 percentage points on the standard ASR metric, from 60.0% (TAP / judge) to 73.3% (TAP / hybrid). All other attacker hyperparameters are fixed; only the per-candidate score function changes.
Why this works: dense gradient vs sparse gradient. The judge is binary (jailbreak / not jailbreak). When TAP branches a leaf into b children, most of them score 0, so the judge ranking becomes near-random and pruning keeps essentially arbitrary leaves. BCA is real-valued in [0, 1] for every candidate; it provides a strict ordering even on prompts the judge would flag as failures. Tree attackers (TAP, with b·w candidates per depth) cash this density into more useful surviving leaves; linear attackers (PAIR, one candidate per stream per step) see fewer candidates and therefore do not benefit — explaining the attacker-geometry-specific reversal where BCA hurts PAIR but helps TAP.
The PAIR row is informative too. Under PAIR (linear), swapping the judge for BCA hurts: 50.0% → 40.0% on judge-ASR. So BCA-as-pruning is not a free win — it is a tree-search-specific improvement, and the result is the kind of attacker-loss interaction that ASR-only benchmarking cannot see. A practitioner reading this table would know to use BCA inside TAP-style attackers and not bother with it inside PAIR-style ones.
GCG note. GCG hit 0% judge-ASR at 200 steps × 256-wide search on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The cell has no BCA variant because BCA is not differentiable through the bounded DTMC, so there is no gradient to substitute. We include GCG only as a compute reference: the strongest LLM attacker we measured (TAP / hybrid, 73.3% judge-ASR) used ~5000× fewer target forward passes per behavior than this GCG run.
Headline (single seed, Qwen judge). Inside a tree-search attacker, using the inner-tree BCA as the per-candidate score instead of (or in addition to) the judge score recovers +13.3 percentage points of judge-ASR — the same metric standard jailbreak benchmarks report — on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with no other change to the attacker. The improvement is tree-search-specific and disappears (in fact reverses) under linear refinement.

Update: the +13.3 pp claim under multi-judge and multi-seed

The +13.3 pp headline is one seed, one in-loop judge (Qwen), and 19 behaviors. Once we vary the judge (Axis-1 in-loop multi-judge run on 30 behaviors) and the attacker RNG seed (multi-seed replicates at 30 behaviors / seed using --seed 42 and --seed 43), the picture changes substantially. Per-method judge-ASR is computed with the standard any-leaf-success semantic (a behavior counts as a jailbreak if any leaf in the TAP tree scored 10/10 by the held-out judge, not just the leaf selected as best_objective — the latter would unfairly penalise BCA-pruning which picks leaves by mass, not by judge score). All numbers below are reproduced by analyze_tap_multiseed.py from the per-run JSONs in results/judge_swap/.

  • Judge swap. Re-running TAP with HarmBench as the in-loop judge (so pruning, BCA leaf, and judge-ASR evaluation all share the new judge family) inverts the sign: regular > hybrid by 4.5 pp. Under LlamaGuard the metric saturates and gives no signal.

Honest reading: BCA-as-pruning is not robustly better than judge-pruning across (judge, seed) replicates on the data we currently have. The original 19-behavior +15 pp is plausibly within the noise floor of a stochastic LLM-as-attacker. The narrative-level claim of the paper does not depend on this bonus result, since Pillars 1 and 2 frame GAS as a diagnostic, not as an attacker objective. We will revisit this table if seeds 44–46 land and shift the pooled CI off zero.

Validation Roadmap: Judge, Attacker, and Target Scaling

Every number reported above is evaluator-conditional under a single Qwen2.5-7B semantic judge, a single open-weight target suite (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), and a single attacker axis (templates → PAIR → TAP → GCG). The diagnostic story (Pillar 1 ranking flip, Pillar 2 distributional fragility) is only as strong as the validation along four orthogonal axes. Each axis below names what we have today, what is in progress, and what would falsify the headline claim.

Axis 0 — Metric Validity: bounded Pr[harm] predicts empirical sampled ASR (done)

Before any of the downstream claims (ranking flip, distributional fragility, attack discovery) can stand, the metric itself must do what it says: the bounded continuation probability Pr[harm] over the inner tree should correlate with how often a randomly sampled completion from the same target is judged harmful. If GAS is just a label-flip artifact of the leaf judge, we should see no relationship between bounded mass and empirical ASR under an independent judge.

We test this directly. For every (behavior, template) pair across four targets, we (i) build the bounded continuation tree at depth L = 8 with Qwen2.5-7B as the BCA leaf judge to get Pr[harm], and (ii) sample n = 50 (or 100 for Qwen-1.5B) independent completions at T = 1.0 and score each one with the HarmBench-Mistral-7B classifier — a different judge family from a different organization. We then correlate bounded mass against empirical ASR. This is non-circular: the judge inside the tree and the judge outside are different oracles.

Target model n pairs Spearman ρ p-value Pearson r Top-1 lift
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct 110 (11b × 10t) 0.596 6.4 × 10⁻¹² 0.31 4.54×
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 540 (30b × 18t) 0.733 6.0 × 10⁻⁹² 0.83 7.43×
Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 540 (30b × 18t) 0.611 1.3 × 10⁻⁵⁶ 0.59 2.56×
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 540 (30b × 18t) 0.534 4.6 × 10⁻⁴¹ 0.79 6.73×

Top-1 lift = if you rank a behavior's templates by bounded Pr[harm] and pick only the top-1, how much more often do you find a harmful sampled completion than if you picked a template at random. A lift of 7.43× on Qwen-7B means BCA mass is a near-optimal template-selection oracle even before you sample anything from the target.

Takeaway. Across all four targets, bounded Pr[harm] is a strongly significant, monotone predictor of empirical sampled judge-ASR under an independent HarmBench judge (Spearman ρ ∈ [0.53, 0.73], every p < 10⁻⁴⁰). The two strongest signals (Llama Pearson r = 0.79, Qwen-7B Pearson r = 0.83) come from the targets where bounded mass spans the widest range. GAS is not a leaf-judge artifact — it is a structural property of the target's continuation distribution that generalizes across judges.

Falsification criterion. If any target's Spearman ρ between bounded Pr[harm] and independent-judge empirical ASR were < 0.2 or statistically insignificant, the entire diagnostic story collapses to "the metric ranks templates by what one judge thinks." It doesn't: even the weakest target (Llama) shows ρ = 0.53 with p = 4.6 × 10⁻⁴¹ on 540 (behavior, template) pairs.

Axis 1 — Judge Robustness: GAS ranking stability across harm classifiers

The judge is a probability-thresholding device, not ground truth. If a different judge flips the per-behavior harm label, GAS@q changes — but the diagnostic claim is that the per-model ranking under GAS is stable across judges. The validation plan replaces the single Qwen judge with a panel and reports both cross-judge agreement and GAS ranking stability.

Judge Type Role Status
Qwen2.5-7B-Instructopen-weight LLM-judge (10/10 score)Primary judge used in all current numbersin use
HarmBench-Mistral-7B classifier (Mazeika et al., 2024)fine-tuned 7B binary classifierStandard benchmark judge — independent of the Qwen familyeval-judge done (Axis 0); in-loop run done (TAP, n=30)
Llama Guard 3 (Inan et al., 2023)policy-trained 8B safety classifierProduction-style content moderation judgein-loop run done — saturates at 100% (not discriminative)
ShieldGemma (Google)2B/9B/27B safety classifier familyIndependent-vendor judge — different training data distributionplanned
GPT-4o / Claude-Sonnet judgeclosed-frontier LLM-judgeUpper-bound / oracle-style judge for agreement ceilingconditional on API budget

Two artifacts the panel will produce:

  • Judge agreement table. Pairwise Cohen's κ on a held-out sample of (prompt, response) pairs, plus per-pair label-flip rates. ICLR-2026 work like AMIS (100% ASR on Claude-4-Sonnet via co-evolved judge templates) shows that judge choice is itself an attack surface — quantifying agreement is mandatory.
  • GAS ranking stability. Per-model GAS@0, GAS@18, GAS@PAIR(3), GAS@TAP(12) under each judge in the panel. We report (i) Spearman ρ of model rankings across judges and (ii) whether the Pillar-1 ranking flip and the Pillar-2 Mistral-vs-Llama gap survive the worst-case judge swap. If the flip survives under all four judges, the claim is judge-robust; if it survives under three but fails under one, that one is documented and discussed.

Falsification criterion. Pillar 1 fails if the Qwen-7B vs Llama-3.1-8B ranking flip reverses under any judge in the panel. Pillar 2 fails if the Mistral GAS@0 ≈ 0.21 number drops below ~0.05 under any judge (i.e., the bounded mass is judge-specific noise rather than a structural property of Mistral's continuation distribution).

We re-ran TAP-Llama-3.1-8B × {regular, bca, hybrid} × 30 JailbreakBench behaviors three times, each time swapping the in-loop judge (used both for pruning and as the BCA leaf judge): Qwen2.5-7B, HarmBench-Mistral-7B, and Llama Guard 3. Each tree is then scored by its own in-loop judge — the diagonal of the cross-judge matrix below.

TAP pruning method Qwen → Qwen-eval HarmBench → HB-eval Llama Guard 3 → LG-eval
regular (judge only) 66.7% (18/27) 58.3% (14/24) 100% (27/27)
bca (Pr[F harm] only) 55.6% (15/27) 57.7% (15/26) 100% (24/24)

Three takeaways: (a) Qwen-pruning gives the highest ASR for regular and hybrid, (b) HarmBench gives a lower but consistent ASR across methods (~54–58%), and (c) Llama Guard 3 flags every TAP response as unsafe across all 75 valid trees. The third result deserves a dedicated finding below.

Pairwise judge agreement on common (behavior, method) pairs

Judge pair n common pairs Agreement Asymmetry
Qwen vs HarmBench 74 59.5% balanced (Qwen-only 17, HarmBench-only 13)
Qwen vs Llama Guard 3 74 63.5% strictly one-sided (Qwen-only 0, LG-only 27)
HarmBench vs Llama Guard 3 71 57.7% strictly one-sided (HarmBench-only 0, LG-only 30)
Headline 1 — Two reasonable semantic judges disagree on ~40% of TAP outcomes. Qwen2.5-7B and HarmBench-Mistral-7B agree on only 44/74 (behavior, method) pairs (59.5%); disagreement is balanced (17 Qwen-only vs 13 HarmBench-only). The "ASR" for a fixed attack can swing by ±10 percentage points depending on which reasonable judge you ask. This is exactly the judge-conditional ASR variability the ICLR 2026 line of work has been flagging.
Headline 2 — Llama Guard 3 is not a discriminative attack-success judge. Llama Guard 3 flags every TAP response (75/75 valid trees, all three methods) as unsafe. Its disagreement with Qwen and HarmBench is strictly one-sided: LG never says "safe" when the others say "unsafe"; it only ever adds more unsafe labels. This is consistent with Llama Guard's training as a content filter, not an "is this an instance of the behavior" classifier. We recommend against using Llama Guard 3 as the judge in ASR-style benchmarks; under LG everything is unsafe by default, so the metric collapses. This is itself a useful Axis-1 robustness finding: not every "policy-trained safety classifier" is a drop-in for an LLM-as-judge.
Headline 3 — No pruning method dominates across judges. Under Qwen-pruning, regular wins (66.7%); under HarmBench-pruning, bca edges hybrid (57.7% vs 53.8%) and ties regular; under Llama Guard 3, the matrix is saturated and uninformative. The "hybrid > regular" claim of the Bonus result is therefore judge-conditional, and a 5-seed multi-replicate TAP-Llama-Qwen sweep currently running will quantify the run-to-run noise floor; preliminary results show Δ(hybrid − regular) ∈ [−0.04, +0.00] across the first two complete replicates, well within run-to-run variance.

Falsification update. The Pillar-1 ranking flip remains intact under HarmBench pruning (the flip is across models, and HarmBench preserves the qualitative ordering on Llama; the matched experiment on Qwen-7B targets is the next step). The Llama Guard 3 axis is a fail — but a useful fail, since it falsifies the silently-held premise that any safety classifier is interchangeable.

Axis 2 — Attack Method Scaling: templates → PAIR → TAP → GCG → AutoDAN → AMIS

Pillar 1's ranking flip is between two attacker types. The validation question is whether the flip is a property of those two attackers or of the attacker-capability axis itself. We trace GAS@q along an attacker ladder of increasing sophistication and report the GAS curve and ranking at each rung.

AutoDAN (Liu et al., 2023)stealthy hierarchical genetic searchblack-box, semantically-natural suffixplanned

ARMs (Chen et al., ICLR'26)adaptive multimodal red-teaming agentorchestrated multi-strategymultimodal, out of scope here

Falsification criterion. If GAS@AutoDAN(q) ranks all four models in the same order as GAS@PAIR(q) and GAS@TAP(q), the attacker axis collapses and Pillar 1's query-budgeted framing is overfit to two attackers. If AutoDAN produces yet another ranking, the attacker axis is multi-dimensional — and that itself is the headline.

Axis 3 — Target Model Coverage: logprob-exposing open-weight systems including gpt-oss

The inner bounded-continuation tree requires per-token logprobs from the target. Closed API models (GPT-4o, Claude) expose only top-k logprobs over the first sampled token, which is insufficient for the α-k expansion. We therefore restrict to open-weight, logprob-exposing targets. The current suite covers four; OpenAI's gpt-oss release (Wallace et al., ICLR 2026, rXLRyJXSCy) is the first open-weight system that explicitly ships under a worst-case-frontier-risk methodology, and is the natural next target.

The gpt-oss row is the analytically interesting one: OpenAI's MFT release methodology explicitly frames the open-weight question as "what worst-case capability does this model release add to the frontier?" GAS measures a different worst-case quantity — distributional reachability of harm under a query-budgeted attacker — and the two diagnostics are complementary. The gpt-oss safety story uses ASR-style capability evals; pairing them with GAS@q gives the first probability-aware reading of an OpenAI-released open-weight model.

Limitations and Open Problems

What this is not. Not a proof of safety. Not a guarantee over the full unbounded output distribution. Not a replacement for broad red-teaming. The right claim is narrower: for a given prompt, model, decoding process, horizon, and evaluator, this method estimates how much of the model's likely continuation mass reaches harmful states. That narrower claim is still useful because most real evaluation pipelines observe only a handful of sampled outputs.

Several hard problems bound the current scope:

  • Evaluator quality. If the harm classifier is weak, the probability estimate is weak. The evaluator is a core bottleneck, not a solved sub-problem.
  • Exponential cost. Tree expansion remains exponential in k and L even with GPU parallelism and prefix caching. Exact bounded DTMC mode (k=2, L=8) is tractable; larger settings require SMC or node-budget truncation.
  • Tail risk. Top-k truncation ignores low-probability outputs. For rare catastrophic events, adversarial search over the tail may be more informative than bounded high-probability expansion.
  • Locality. The method is local to a specific prompt and decoding configuration. It does not certify global model behavior.
  • Prefix ambiguity. A prefix may appear harmless until later tokens make it actionable, complicating intermediate labeling at non-leaf nodes.

Natural extensions: adaptive expansion near risky branches; probability-mass bounds for the unexplored tail; property-directed search (expand only toward harmful states); combining SMC with adversarial prompt generation; using extracted harmful branches as seeds for adversarial training or patch validation.

Conclusion

Standard jailbreak evaluation asks whether one sampled response is harmful. The ICLR 2026 attack landscape — adaptive multimodal red-teamers, co-evolved attacker/judge meta-optimizers, agentic-search frameworks — has already moved past that question. We propose Generative-Attack Susceptibility (GAS) as the complementary probability-aware, query-budgeted diagnostic: instead of "did one response break?", it asks "within Q adaptive queries, can the attacker reach a prompt whose bounded continuation tree carries substantial harmful mass?" Two distinct pillars come out of that single reachability question.

  • Pillar 1 — Query-budgeted curves expose ranking flips invisible to ASR. Under a fixed 18-template library, Qwen2.5-7B is the most vulnerable target (GAS@18 = 0.91) and Llama-3.1-8B is the most robust (GAS@18 = 0.14). After 3 PAIR queries the ordering flips: Llama's bounded harmful mass climbs to 0.17 (above its own GAS@18) while Qwen-7B barely moves to 0.02. Model rankings depend on the attacker's query budget; ASR cannot rank these models because the ranking itself is a function of the attacker capability. Per-behavior GAS@18 correlates with empirical full-completion ASR at Spearman ρ = 0.66 on Llama-3.1-8B, so the diagnostic is grounded in the same signal ASR pipelines see — but read more granularly.
  • Pillar 2 — Refusal is not robustness: distributional fragility under matched ASR. Every target has sampled judge-ASR ≈ 0% on the un-jailbroken direct prompt. Under any standard one-shot ASR pipeline, all four models look identically safe. The bounded continuation tree on the same prompt tells a different story: GAS@0 is 0.211 on Mistral-7B vs 0.002 on Llama-3.1-8B — Mistral places ~21% of its bounded-depth continuation mass on harmful leaves while sounding indistinguishable from Llama on the surface. The refusal-collapse probability formalism makes this falsifiable: that bounded mass is conditional on the greedy first token being a refusal marker. ASR collapses this gap; GAS exposes it.
  • Bonus result — GAS as an attacker pruning signal: query- and judge-conditional, not yet robust. Holding TAP fixed and swapping its per-candidate pruning signal from the judge score to a 0.5·judge + 0.5·BCA hybrid raises judge-ASR from 60.0% to 73.3% at matched q = 12 on Llama-3.1-8B (+13.3 pp) on the original 19-behavior single-seed run. The same swap under PAIR (linear refinement) hurts. The Axis-1 in-loop multi-judge re-run at 30 behaviors and a multi-seed sweep both show the gap shrinking to near zero or inverting once we vary the judge or the attacker RNG — provisionally, BCA-as-pruning is not robustly better than judge-pruning across (judge, seed) replicates. We therefore present this as a query- and judge-conditional observation about tree-search attackers in particular, not as a universal claim. The paper's narrative-level story is GAS-as-diagnostic (Pillars 1 and 2); this bonus result is bonus, not load-bearing.
The reframe:
Not "did the model jailbreak?", but "within Q adaptive queries, can the attacker reach a prompt whose bounded continuation tree contains substantial harmful mass?" — a finite-horizon reachability property, evaluated exactly on the inner token tree and by SMC on the outer attacker tree.
Pillar 1 — Query-budgeted ranking: GAS@18: Qwen-7B 0.91 · Qwen-1.5B 0.91 · Mistral 0.78 · Llama 0.14  ·  GAS@PAIR(3): Llama 0.17 (hybrid) · Qwen-7B 0.02 (hybrid)
Pillar 2 — Distributional fragility @ direct prompt (sampled judge-ASR ≈ 0% for all): Mistral GAS@0 0.211 · Qwen-7B 0.004 · Qwen-1.5B 0.004 · Llama 0.002 (~100× spread under matched 0% sampled-ASR)
Bonus — independent judge-ASR @ q_max, Llama-3.1-8B (single seed, Qwen judge): TAP / judge prune 60.0% → TAP / BCA prune 62.5% → TAP / hybrid prune 73.3%  ·  PAIR / judge prune 50.0% (no BCA win under linear refinement)  ·  GCG (200 steps × 256-wide) 0%
Axis 1 in-loop multi-judge audit on TAP-Llama (30 behaviors): Qwen vs HarmBench agree on only 59.5% of (behavior, method) outcomes; Llama Guard 3 saturates at 100% ASR across all 75 valid TAP trees and is documented as unfit as an ASR-style judge. The +13.3 pp bonus result shrinks to −3.7 pp under HarmBench-pruning and to ±0 pp on a second Qwen seed, so it is reported as a tree-search-specific, evaluator-conditional finding rather than a robust claim.
Headline Pillar-1 and Pillar-2 numbers above are evaluator-conditional under a Qwen2.5-7B judge held fixed across all attackers and targets. Axis-0 metric validity is established under an independent HarmBench classifier. Remaining judge-robustness, attacker-scaling (AutoDAN, AMIS), and target-scaling (gpt-oss) audits are documented in the validation roadmap.
